title: Sustained Beauty and Splendor:  Aristotle and Homer
author: Evaggelos Vallianatos
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-
image-421207-1.jpeg)

Aristotle with a bust of Homer by Rembrandt, 1653. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Public Domain.

I have a deep respect and affection for Homer. I do indeed think of him as the
teacher of the Greeks. My understanding of Homer is no different than that of
ancient Greeks.

In a metaphorical way, I am ancient Greek, too. In Greek, ancient is _αρχαῖος
/ archaios,_ which means more than very old. Its core meaning is beginning and
the rule of law.

**Homer: sparked Greek civilization**

The ancient Greeks started what we call civilization. And Homer was the spark
for that Promethean transformation of the Greeks. Plato would not disagree. He
thought Homer was “the best poet and the most divine” (Ion 530c). He also
reports that during the _Panathenaea_ , Athens’ quadrennial religious and
athletic festival honoring the birthdate of goddess Athena, bards would sing
extensively from the poetry of Homer. Such public performances of the Homeric
epics took place in the theater of Dionysos in front of about 20,000 Athenians
who, along with the bards, wept while listening to the story-songs of Homer
(Ion 530c; 535d-e).

**Homer the Poet**

Aristotle had no doubt that Homer was “the poet of poets” (Poetics 48b 30-35).
He was the first scholar-philosopher who decoded the wisdom of Homer. He
realized that Homer’s epics revealed a secret and lost knowledge of Bronze Age
Mycenaean Greece. He understood the importance of that knowledge. No wonder
Aristotle treated Homer as an equal. He often mentioned him in his
philosophical, scientific and political works.

**Homer the polymath**

Homer was a polymath. His poetry is full of gems of wisdom and insights about
the Greeks, the Trojans, war, peace, agriculture, geography, traditions,
science, technology (robots, very advanced technology), the natural world, the
Cosmos, and the gods. Aristotle was also a polymath. Reading the epics of
Homer was like going through an encyclopedia of tremendous wisdom and
knowledge of great antiquity.

To Aristotle, Homer was like a fountain of knowledge and lighthouse of wisdom.
His epics were like a time machine, allowing Aristotle to see the Cosmos and
Greek society about 900 years before his age, the fourth century BCE. Homer
gave Aristotle satisfaction, pleasure, and probable confirmation of his own
knowledge, wisdom, and science.

**Scientific insights from Homer**

For example, Aristotle refers to Homer several times in his most important
scientific treatise, _History of Animals._ In one instance (519a 10-20), he
examined the potential influence of drinking water on the color of the hair of
animals. Aristotle suspected that water quality might explain why sheep
grazing the Chalcidian Peninsula on the coast of Thrace gave birth to lambs
that were sometimes white and other times black.

Scamander River, surrounding Troy, made the hair of lambs yellow, which,
Aristotle says, convinced Homer to name Scamander the Yellow River.

At another section of the _History of Animals_ (575a), Aristotle discusses the
age of Laconian / Spartan dogs. The males lived for about ten years. The
females, however, lived for fourteen and sometimes twenty years.

This realization prompted Aristotle to bring up Homer and the account in the
_Odyssey_ (17.326) that Odysseus’s dog Argos died at the age of twenty.

In similar fashion, Aristotle cites Homer in his _Politics, Poetics,
Nicomachean Ethics,_ and other philosophical works. For example, in his
_Nicomachean Ethics_(1141a 12-29). Aristotle goes to Homer in confirming his
notion of wisdom, that is, wisdom is a combination of “intuitive reason and
scientific knowledge.”

Another example when the Philosopher merged his observation of nature with
that of Homer comes from book XXIII of _Problems_ (934a 13-24). Aristotle had
observed that still water was more transparent than moving water, so the color
of the sea changed from blue to almost black. Homer, Aristotle said, had
reached a similar conclusion, saying the wind moved the water to a darker
color, eventually capturing the metaphor in Homer’s work of the wine-dark sea
(_Odyssey_ 12.388).

Moreover, Aristotle has no doubt that Homer was the supreme poet of Hellas,
with inestimable contributions to the development of poetry and tragedy and
theater.

Aristotle was by far the most profound of Greek thinkers. He had no doubt that
Homer was the god-like author of the _Iliad_ and the _Odyssey_. He had no
doubt that those epics were primarily the early history of the Greek people.
Much more than any modern classical scholar, Aristotle had access to
information and knowledge about Homer. Like the rest of the Greeks, the
Philosopher judged Homer to be the teacher of the Greeks and a seminal pillar
of Hellenic civilization.

**Singing Homer**

About 700 years after Aristotle, another Greek thinker spoke about Homer. This
was Diogenes Laertios, a writer and philosopher. He flourished in the first
half of the third century. He said that, from around 600 BCE, rhapsodes
recited the poems of Homer all over the Greek world. This was especially true
at the islands of Chios, Cyprus and Delos and the poleis / city-states of
Syracuse in Magna Graecia, Sicyon in Peloponnesos, and Athens.

The recitation of the Homeric epics in Athens coincided with the celebration
of Dionysos in both Athens and Brauron in the countryside of Attica. Solon,
who was archon/leader of Athens in 594 BCE, required that rhapsodes, singers
of poetry, sing substantive continuous sections of the poems of Homer, rather
than disconnected passages (Diogenes Laertios, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
1.57).

**History, sustained beauty and splendor in Homer**

There’s some fiction in the epics of Homer, but not enough to dilute the
historical integrity of the stories. Homer, inspired by the Muses/goddesses of
learning, set down in alphabetic Greek writing the early history of the
Greeks, a poetic account that records historical events dating from the early
Bronze Age or more than 5,000 years ago.

The Roman teacher of rhetoric, Quintilian (Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, who
flourished in the first century), captured the essence and appreciation of
Homer in the Western tradition. “Homer,” he says, “is like his own conception
of the Ocean, which he describes as the source of every stream and river; for
he has given us a model and an inspiration for every department of
eloquence…no one has ever surpassed him in the sublimity with which he invests
great themes or the propriety with which he handles small themes. He is at
once luxuriant and concise, sprightly, and serious, remarkable at once for his
fullness and his brevity, and supreme not merely for poetic, but for
oratorical power as well…. the Poet was the master of all” (Training in
Oratory 10.1.46-51, tr. Moses Hades, Ancilla to Classical Reading, New York:
Columbia University Press, 1954, 143-144).

Nineteen centuries after Quintilian, J. A. K. Thomson, a rare American Homeric
scholar, connects the epics of Homer to the very foundations of the West. He
mirrors Aristotle and Quintilian. “At the sources of Western civilization,” he
says, “themselves its main source, stand two poems on the grand scale which
for sustained beauty and splendor have found no superior, perhaps no equal, in
all the poetry that has followed them. This is the most remarkable fact in the
history of literature. If it seems to contradict what Aristotle regards as
almost a law of nature – that the arts progress by degrees – we may discover
the explanation in this, that the _Iliad_ and the _Odysse_ y are not the
beginning but the consummation of an artistic process of which the earliest
stages are no longer discernible. But, while this would explain the fact, it
does not explain the miracle. The miracle is the quality of the poetry, and
miracles cannot be explained” (“Homer and his Influence” in A Companion to
Homer, eds., Alan J.B. Wace and Frank H. Stubbing’s, New York: The Macmillan
Company, 1963, 1).

**Epilogue**

Aristotle, Quintilian and Thomson give us a balanced view of Homer, the great
poet, teacher and historian of Bronze Age Hellenic civilization. This view
rejects the mostly biased perspectives of classical scholars and movie
producers like Christopher Nolan, who present Homer as a fiction writer.
